analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on offshore tax havens and abusive tax shelters used to dodge federal taxes.
analysis.headline: Despite 78 House sponsors, the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act never received a hearing or a vote in any committee and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it harder for wealthy individuals and large corporations to hide money offshore or run abusive tax shelters. It would let the Treasury restrict foreign banks and jurisdictions that block U.S. tax enforcement, treat foreign corporations actually managed from the U.S. as domestic for tax purposes, force public country-by-country reporting of where multinationals earn and pay tax, tighten money-laundering rules for hedge funds and company-formation agents, and raise penalties for tax-shelter promoters and advisers charging contingency fees. It was referred to two House committees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently make up the difference when the wealthy and corporations shift income offshore; honest domestic businesses that compete against firms using shell entities; and state and federal governments that lose revenue to offshore avoidance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and honest competing businesses

how_it_helps.text: Treasury could cut off correspondent accounts and payment cards for foreign banks or jurisdictions that impede U.S. tax enforcement, not just money launderers.

Transactions with banks that refuse to comply with foreign-account reporting (FATCA) would face a presumption that they generate taxable income or indicate control, shifting the burden onto the offshore account holder to prove otherwise.
Foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily from the United States would be taxed as domestic corporations, closing the 'foreign' shell trick for firms with $50 million or more in assets.
SEC-registered corporations would have to report employees, sales, profits, and taxes paid in every country where they operate, making it visible when profits are booked in tax havens.

Hedge funds and private equity funds would have to run anti-money-laundering programs and file suspicious-activity reports, and business-formation agents would face the same rules, closing a common route for hiding ownership.

Penalties for promoting abusive tax shelters or helping understate tax liability would rise to up to 150% of the promoter's gross income, the penalties would no longer be tax-deductible, and contingency fees tied to 'tax savings' would be banned.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy individuals using offshore accounts, multinational corporations that would face new public reporting and possible domestic tax treatment, financial institutions and hedge funds facing new compliance and reporting duties, and tax advisers who profit from shelter promotion.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy offshore users and big finance

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes significant new reporting and compliance costs on banks, brokers, hedge funds, and company-formation agents, which could be passed on to customers and investors.

The rebuttable presumptions shift the burden of proof to the taxpayer in cases involving non-FATCA institutions, raising the risk that legitimate cross-border business arrangements get swept into disputes with the IRS.
Country-by-country reporting requires detailed disclosure of operations and tax payments in every jurisdiction, which multinationals argue is costly and competitively sensitive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — recovering revenue and enforcement leverage against offshore evasion, with the cost falling on those using the schemes — outweighs the compliance burdens, which are real but concentrated on the firms and individuals the bill targets. The burden-shifting presumptions are aggressive and could entangle some legitimate transactions, but they apply only to dealings with institutions that refuse standard international reporting.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, passed down to subcommittees a month later, and then simply sat there until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act on July 27, 2011, with 77 Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee on the day of introduction.
In August 2011 it was referred to two subcommittees — Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and Capital Markets — and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill died at the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013, without any vote in committee or on the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Users of offshore tax havens and tax shelters — wealthy individuals, hedge funds, multinationals, and the banks and advisers that service them — kept the status quo because no committee ever acted on the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore finance and its wealthy clients

for.name: Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 53 original cosponsors.

for.name: 77 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee with jurisdiction over most of the bill's tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred in July 2011.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee with jurisdiction over the securities and money-laundering provisions
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees in August 2011 and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 78 supporters were House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, and the bill sat in committees controlled by the Republican majority until it died.

industries.note: The bill lets Treasury cut off their access to U.S. correspondent accounts and card networks if they impede tax enforcement, and treats dealings with non-cooperating institutions as presumptively taxable. Their business of servicing hidden offshore money costs ordinary taxpayers revenue.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity funds
industries.note: They would face mandatory anti-money-laundering programs, suspicious-activity reports, and beneficial-ownership reporting for foreign-controlled accounts. Secrecy around fund money flows is part of what enables offshore avoidance.

industries.industry: Tax shelter promoters and tax advisory firms
industries.note: Penalties for promoting abusive shelters and aiding understatement would rise to 150% of gross income from the activity, become non-deductible, and contingency fees based on 'tax savings' would be banned. Their product is tax savings that shift the burden onto other taxpayers.

They would have to disclose employees, sales, and taxes paid in every country, and foreign corporations managed from the U.S. would be taxed as domestic. Public country-by-country data exposes profit-shifting to tax havens.
Forming shell companies would become a money-laundering-regulated business requiring customer identification programs. Shell entities are the basic building block of offshore secrecy.
